sipnab reads the SIP and the audio that pass through Asterisk off the wire, so
it needs nothing from Asterisk: no module, no configuration change. Asterisk is
a [B2BUA](@/docs/glossary.md#b2bua): every call through it is two SIP calls, called
legs, the caller's leg into Asterisk and Asterisk's leg out to the callee, each
with its own Call-ID. sipnab lists the two legs as two
[dialogs](@/docs/glossary.md#dialog), shows them together as one call flow, and
measures the audio on each.

This guide adds sipnab to the Asterisk machine from
[Use Asterisk as your voice stack's PBX](@/docs/asterisk.md): it watches a test call,
shows its two legs in the terminal interface, explains it from a saved
capture, answers about it over MCP and the REST API, and finally receives
Asterisk's own copies of its SIP over HEP.

**What works without Asterisk.** sipnab does not depend on Asterisk. Steps 2
to 6 use sipnab's own capture and work the same way beside any SIP server.
Step 7 is the one that uses an Asterisk module, and you can leave it out.

## Tested on

Every block on this page ran as written, in order, on 2026-10-12, with sipnab
0.5.211 from its release package, on the Debian 13 (kernel 6.12.63) and Ubuntu
24.04 (kernel 6.8.0) machines that [the Asterisk guide](@/docs/asterisk.md) had set
up. The terminal interface ran in a terminal 160 columns wide and 40 lines
high, with the test call placed while it ran, and the keys in step 3 showed
what that step describes. Every test call carried audio both ways. On both,
causing each fault under [When something does not
work](#when-something-does-not-work) produced the message it quotes.

The examples use `192.0.2.10` as the machine's address. Replace it with yours
everywhere it appears.

## 1. Install sipnab

```bash
# Run all of these, in order.
V=$(curl -fsSL https://api.github.com/repos/NormB/sipnab/releases/latest \
  | python3 -c 'import json,sys; print(json.load(sys.stdin)["tag_name"].lstrip("v"))')
curl -fsSLO https://github.com/NormB/sipnab/releases/download/v$V/sipnab_${V}_amd64.deb
curl -fsSL https://github.com/NormB/sipnab/releases/download/v$V/SHA256SUMS.txt \
  | grep " sipnab_${V}_amd64.deb$" | sha256sum -c -
sudo apt-get install -y ./sipnab_${V}_amd64.deb jq
sipnab --version
```

The commands in steps 4 to 6 use `jq` to pick fields out of sipnab's JSON, so
the block installs it too.

## 2. Watch a call through Asterisk

Start sipnab on every interface for 30 seconds. It prints each SIP message as
it passes and a report of the calls at the end, and `-O` saves every packet it
captured to `/tmp/asterisk-call.pcap` for steps 4 and 5:

```bash
sudo sipnab -N -d any --duration 30 --report -O /tmp/asterisk-call.pcap
```

While it runs, place a test call from a second terminal, as in
[step 3 of the Asterisk guide](@/docs/asterisk.md#3-place-a-test-call):

```bash
# Run all of these, in order.
cd ~/sipp
sipp -sf uas.xml -i 192.0.2.10 -p 5070 -min_rtp_port 7000 -max_rtp_port 7100 -rtp_echo -m 1 -bg
sudo sipp -sn uac_pcap 192.0.2.10:5060 -i 192.0.2.10 -p 5080 -s 100 -m 1 -timeout 90s
```

sipnab prints the caller's `INVITE` to Asterisk at `192.0.2.10:5060`, then
Asterisk's own `INVITE` to the callee at `192.0.2.10:5070`, with a Call-ID
Asterisk generated and an SDP offer of its own. When the 30 seconds are up, the
report lists the two legs as two calls, both `Completed` with code `200`:

```text
Call-ID                          From           To             State        Code   Duration   Msgs   PDD      Tags
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
1-50232@192.0.2.10               sipp           100            Completed    200    9s         7      0.0s     -
37e58306-c14d-4a0f-9fa1-41a...   sipp           -              Completed    200    9s         6      0.0s     -
```

The first is the caller's leg, to extension `100`, with 7 messages, among
them Asterisk's `100 Trying` to the caller. The second is Asterisk's leg to the
callee, with 6. Its `To` column shows `-` because Asterisk addressed the callee
as `<sip:192.0.2.10>`, with no user name.

Below them, the `RTP Streams:` table shows that the audio goes through
Asterisk, in a different codec on each leg:

- On the caller's leg, 236 `PCMA` packets from the caller to Asterisk, and 236
  `PCMA` packets back, the callee's echo.
- On the callee's leg, 236 `PCMU` packets each way between Asterisk and the
  callee: Asterisk converts the caller's PCMA to PCMU, which is the only codec
  the callee takes.
- The caller's key press, 10 `telephone-event` (DTMF) packets to Asterisk.
  Asterisk passes it to the callee as a tone inside the audio, so the callee's
  leg carries no `telephone-event` stream. After the key press, both legs show
  short PCMU and PCMA streams under new SSRCs: 6 `PCMU` packets each way on
  the callee's leg, and 10 `PCMA` packets toward the caller.

## 3. See both legs as one call flow

The terminal interface shows the same calls, and updates as they happen:

```bash
sudo sipnab -d any
```

Place the test call from a second terminal, as in step 2. The call list shows
two rows, one per leg, both `Completed`, with 7 and 6 messages. Then, in the
terminal interface:

- **Press `F4`** with the first row selected. The extended flow draws both
  legs in one ladder with three columns, the caller at `192.0.2.10:5080`,
  Asterisk at `192.0.2.10:5060` and the callee at `192.0.2.10:5070`: the
  caller's `INVITE` to Asterisk, Asterisk's `INVITE` to the callee, the
  callee's answer, and Asterisk's answer to the caller, in the order they
  happened. Press `Esc` to go back to the list.
- **Press `Space`, `↓` (the down arrow), `Space` again, then `Enter`.**
  `Space` stars the selected row, so this stars both legs. With two rows
  starred, `Enter` opens one flow of both, in time order: the same
  three-column ladder. Press `Esc` to go back to the list.
- **Press `Tab`** for the RTP streams. Each stream names the leg it belongs
  to in the `Dialog` column.

Press `q`, then `y`, to quit.

## 4. Explain the call from the saved capture

`--call-report` explains one call: its SIP transactions with their timings,
and for each audio stream its packets, jitter, loss and estimated
[MOS](@/docs/glossary.md#mos) (call quality on a scale from 1 to 5). Reading a file
needs no root. The first line finds the caller's leg in the capture from step
2:

```bash
# Run all of these, in order.
CALL=$(sipnab -N -I /tmp/asterisk-call.pcap --json-dialogs --no-cli-print | jq -r 'select(.to == "100") | .call_id')
sipnab -N -I /tmp/asterisk-call.pcap --call-report "$CALL" --no-cli-print
```

The report covers the caller's leg. Its `SIP Transactions` show the `INVITE`
answered in a few milliseconds, then the `ACK`, and the `BYE` 9 seconds later:

```text
SIP Transactions:
  INVITE -> 100 -> 180 (1ms) -> 200 (3ms)
  ACK
  BYE -> 200 (9008ms)
```

Under `Media Streams`, the two PCMA streams of 236 packets, one each way, show
no loss and `mos=4.36 R=90.8`. The `telephone-event` stream shows
`mos=unknown (unpublished)`: sipnab gives no quality estimate for DTMF events.
The last stream is the 10 PCMA packets toward the caller. The report ends with
`Issues Detected: None`.

## 5. Ask about the call over MCP

sipnab's MCP server lets an AI agent ask about a capture. The [MCP
guide](@/docs/mcp.md) sets it up for a client. This block sends the three messages a
client would, straight from the shell, and asks `find_correlated` which other
leg belongs to the caller's call. The first line takes the caller's Call-ID
from the report, from the row whose `To` is `100`:

```bash
# Run all of these, in order.
CALL=$(sipnab -N -I /tmp/asterisk-call.pcap --report --no-cli-print | awk '$3 == "100" {print $1}')
printf '%s\n' \
  '{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":1,"method":"initialize","params":{"protocolVersion":"2025-06-18","capabilities":{},"clientInfo":{"name":"shell","version":"0"}}}' \
  '{"jsonrpc":"2.0","method":"notifications/initialized"}' \
  "{\"jsonrpc\":\"2.0\",\"id\":2,\"method\":\"tools/call\",\"params\":{\"name\":\"find_correlated\",\"arguments\":{\"call_id\":\"$CALL\"}}}" \
  | sipnab --mcp -N -I /tmp/asterisk-call.pcap --quiet \
  | jq 'select(.id == 2) | .result.content[0].text | fromjson | {total_matched, heuristic_only, legs}'
```

The answer names Asterisk's leg:

```json
{
  "total_matched": 1,
  "heuristic_only": true,
  "legs": [
    {
      "call_id": "37e58306-c14d-4a0f-9fa1-41a2b3c05f96",
      "identifier_match": false,
      "observed_gap_ms": 1,
      "score": 50,
      "strategy": "timing_heuristic"
    }
  ]
}
```

`timing_heuristic` means that sipnab matched the legs because they share an
address and started within 2 seconds of each other, here 1 millisecond apart
(`observed_gap_ms`). That is a guess, and the answer says so:
`identifier_match` is false and `heuristic_only` is true. Asterisk puts no
header on its leg that names the caller's leg, so sipnab has no identifier to
match on.

## 6. Keep sipnab running, and query it over REST

The sipnab package installs a systemd service, `sipnab`, which captures on
every interface without the terminal interface. Turn on its REST API. sipnab
reads the API key from the environment, and keeping the key in a file only
root can read keeps it out of the command line, where every user on the
machine could read it:

```bash
# Run all of these, in order.
sudo sh -c 'umask 077; printf "SIPNAB_API_KEY=%s\n" "$(openssl rand -hex 32)" > /etc/sipnab/api.env'
sudo mkdir -p /etc/systemd/system/sipnab.service.d
sudo tee /etc/systemd/system/sipnab.service.d/api.conf >/dev/null <<'EOF'
[Service]
EnvironmentFile=/etc/sipnab/api.env
ExecStart=
ExecStart=/usr/bin/sipnab -N -d any --no-cli-print --syslog --metrics 127.0.0.1:9090 --api 127.0.0.1:8080
EOF
sudo systemctl daemon-reload
sudo systemctl enable --now sipnab
systemctl is-active sipnab
```

The `ExecStart` line keeps the package's own arguments and adds `--api`. The
API listens on `127.0.0.1` only.

Place the test call again, as in step 2. Then ask sipnab for its calls, the
leg that goes with the caller's, and the audio streams:

```bash
# Run all of these, in order.
KEY=$(sudo sed -n 's/^SIPNAB_API_KEY=//p' /etc/sipnab/api.env)
curl -s -H "Authorization: Bearer $KEY" 127.0.0.1:8080/v1/dialogs \
  | jq -r '.dialogs[] | [.call_id, .to_user // "-", .state, .msg_count] | @tsv'
CALL=$(curl -s -H "Authorization: Bearer $KEY" 127.0.0.1:8080/v1/dialogs | jq -r '.dialogs[] | select(.to_user == "100") | .call_id')
curl -s -H "Authorization: Bearer $KEY" "127.0.0.1:8080/v1/dialogs/$CALL/correlated" | jq -c '.legs[]'
curl -s -H "Authorization: Bearer $KEY" 127.0.0.1:8080/v1/streams \
  | jq -r '.streams[] | [.associated_dialog, .codec, .packets, .loss_pct] | @tsv'
```

The first answer lists the two legs, `Completed` with 7 and 6 messages. The
second names Asterisk's leg with `"strategy":"timing_heuristic"`, as MCP did
in step 5. The third lists each stream with the leg it belongs to, its codec,
its packets and its loss. The [REST API reference](@/docs/api.md) gives every
route.

## 7. Receive Asterisk's HEP

[HEP](@/docs/glossary.md#hep) is the protocol SIP servers use to send a copy of their
traffic to a collector such as Homer. Asterisk sends HEP with its `res_hep`
module, which the build in the Asterisk guide includes, and sipnab can receive
it. sipnab then sees the SIP as Asterisk handled it, with no capture on the
wire. Point Asterisk at sipnab's HEP listener, on port 9060 of the loopback
address, and restart it:

```bash
# Run all of these, in order.
sudo tee /etc/asterisk/hep.conf >/dev/null <<'EOF'
[general]
enabled = yes
capture_address = 127.0.0.1:9060
capture_id = 1234
uuid_type = call-id
EOF
sudo systemctl restart asterisk
until sudo asterisk -rx 'core waitfullybooted' 2>/dev/null; do sleep 1; done
sudo asterisk -rx 'module show like hep'
```

The `until` line waits for Asterisk to finish starting, as in
[step 2 of the Asterisk guide](@/docs/asterisk.md#2-configure-asterisk).
`module show like hep` lists `res_hep.so`, `res_hep_pjsip.so` and
`res_hep_rtcp.so` as `Running`. `capture_id` is the number Asterisk stamps on
every copy it sends, so that a collector can tell its senders apart. `uuid_type
= call-id` labels each copy with the SIP Call-ID.

Start sipnab's HEP listener for 30 seconds:

```bash
sudo sipnab -N -L 127.0.0.1:9060 --duration 30 --report --hep-senders
```

While it runs, place the test call from a second terminal, as in step 2.
sipnab prints each message as it arrives, marked `origin=hep`. When the 30
seconds are up, the report lists the same two legs, and who sent them:

```text
  SOURCE                                PACKETS  LAST SEEN                    IDLE  STATE
  hep:1234@127.0.0.1                         15  2026-10-12T07:52:29.691Z      14s  sending
```

`hep:1234` is Asterisk's `capture_id`. The last line counts `15 packets
captured, 13 SIP messages`. The other two packets are RTCP summaries from
`res_hep_rtcp`, which Asterisk sends as JSON, and sipnab's report shows nothing
from them. HEP carries no audio, so this report has no `RTP Streams:` table.
For the audio, capture on the wire as in step 2.

HEP over UDP carries no authentication of its own, and the capture id is what
the sender claims. Listening on `127.0.0.1` keeps every sender but this
machine out.

## Remove what this guide added

```bash
# Run all of these, in order.
sudo systemctl disable --now sipnab
sudo apt-get purge -y sipnab
sudo rm -rf /etc/systemd/system/sipnab.service.d /etc/sipnab
sudo systemctl daemon-reload
sudo rm -f /etc/asterisk/hep.conf /tmp/asterisk-call.pcap
sudo systemctl restart asterisk
```

`apt-get purge` removes the package and its own configuration. The API key
file and the drop-in are yours, so the block removes them. The package leaves
the `sipnab` user in place.

## When something does not work

- **sipnab says `sipnab: the terminal UI could not start: No such device or
  address (os error 6). It needs a terminal; add -N for a run without one.`**
  The terminal interface needs an interactive terminal, and this session has
  none, as with a command passed to `ssh` without `-t`. Run it from an
  interactive login, or use `-N` as in step 2.
- **sipnab's HEP listener ends with `HEP listener on 127.0.0.1:9060 finished: 0
  packets received`.** Asterisk sent nothing. Run `sudo asterisk -rx 'module
  show like hep'`: if the three modules show `Not Running`, Asterisk has not
  read `hep.conf`. `core reload` does not start them; restart Asterisk.
- **The REST API answers
  `{"status":401,"title":"Unauthorized","type":"https://sipnab.com/problems/unauthorized"}`.**
  The request carried no API key, or the wrong one. Read it from
  `/etc/sipnab/api.env`, as in step 6.
